title: Earth's magnetic field
summary: Earth's magnetic field is generated in its liquid iron core and protects the atmosphere from solar winds that could strip it away, along with the water that makes life possible. Since 2010, the best estimate of its age had been 3.45 billion years, but measurements on Jack Hills zircons suggest it is about 500 million years older. A listed study of rocks in Australia reports a core dynamo at 3.5 billion years ago.

uncertainty.note: Paleointensity studies from the Barberton Greenstone Belt and Pilbara Craton constrain an active core geodynamo between 3.5 and 3.45 Ga.

where.modern_name: No single place; stand-in pin at Barberton, South Africa
where.historical_name: Kaapvaal Craton, Paleoarchean crust; no modern polities or geographical entities existed

paleo.not_applicable: Deep time planetary geodynamo operating in Earth's liquid iron outer core; surface proxy pin on Kaapvaal Craton.

importance.justification: The geomagnetic field generated by Earth's core geodynamo shields the atmosphere and oceans from solar wind stripping, establishing a vital precondition for planetary habitability.

sources.title: Plate motion and a dipolar geomagnetic field at 3.25 Ga
sources.author: Alec R. Brenner, Roger R. Fu, Andrew R. Kylander-Clark, George J. Hudak, Bradford J. Foley

sources.title: Researchers find that Earth’s magnetic shield is 500 million years older than previously thought
sources.author: Peter Iglinski

reviewer_note: Its true age is debated, and these two sources give different dates. The pin at Barberton is a stand-in, because the field is planet-wide.
